policies.title: Act 2026-610 (SB 270) — large-load data center utility contract review
key_terms: Applies to 'large load data centers' with 150 MW or more of peak demand
Requires Alabama Public Service Commission review of utility contracts with these customers to ensure cost recovery for the incremental service provided
Contracts must demonstrate positive benefits for other utility customers (e.g. lower costs, improved system efficiency, or community economic growth)
Passed both chambers unanimously April 9, 2026 (via voice vote on the second-to-last day of session); Commission opened a generic proceeding July 8, 2026 to set contract-review procedures
Effective October 1, 2026
policies.summary: Alabama's SB 270 (Act 2026-610), sponsored by Sen. Lance Bell and passed unanimously by both chambers on April 9, 2026, requires the Public Service Commission to review electric-utility contracts with 150 MW+ data centers to ensure the utility recovers the incremental cost of serving them and that the arrangement benefits other ratepayers. It takes effect October 1, 2026; the PSC opened an implementing proceeding July 8, 2026.
policies.source_title: Yahoo News (Alabama Reflector) — Bill that seeks to regulate data center boom in Alabama heads to Governor's desk

resources.title: Alabama Public Service Commission — Docket 33709 Public Comment and Reply Info

policies.title: AWS data center community impact program
key_terms: "AWS is also committed to returning more water to communities and the environment than we use" (water positive by 2030; 41% of the way there by end of 2023)
Committed to net-zero carbon by 2040
More than 80,000 students across the U.S. supported through 93 'Think Big Spaces' STEAM labs
$156 billion invested in U.S. data center infrastructure since 2011, supporting more than 37,000 jobs annually
policies.summary: AWS publishes a standing, ongoing (evergreen, no single announcement date) set of community-impact commitments for its data center regions: water-positive-by-2030 pledge, net-zero-carbon-by-2040 target, STEAM education investment via Think Big Spaces, and region-by-region economic impact reporting (investment, jobs, tax payments) for states such as Virginia, Ohio, and Oregon.
policies.source_title: About Amazon — How Amazon helps data center communities thrive

policies.title: Anthropic: covering electricity price increases from our data centers
key_terms: "We will pay for 100% of the grid upgrades needed to interconnect our data centers, paid through increases to our monthly electricity charges."
"We will work to bring net-new power generation online to match our data centers' electricity needs."
Investing in curtailment systems that cut data center power usage during periods of peak demand
"Our current data center projects will create hundreds of permanent jobs and thousands of construction jobs."
Deploying water-efficient cooling technologies
policies.summary: Anthropic published a company-wide commitment to cover 100% of grid-interconnection upgrade costs for its own-workload data centers (funded via its own electricity charges), to bring net-new power generation online to match demand, to invest in demand curtailment during peak grid stress, and to deploy water-efficient cooling. The company notes it is still exploring how to address impacts at sites where it leases capacity rather than operates directly.
policies.source_title: Anthropic — Covering electricity price increases from our data centers

policies.title: Chapter 111 (HB 2756) — extra high load factor customer reporting and contract terms
key_terms: Applies to 'extra high load factor customers' (large loads like data centers) served by public power entities with 1M+ connections and by electric service corporations (excluding those serving 40,000 or fewer connections)
Requires semiannual reports to the governing body/Corporation Commission on the number of interconnection requests and completed interconnections for new extra high load factor customers
Corporation Commission may set minimum bills, contract length, early-termination provisions, collateral requirements and customer payment obligations for necessary infrastructure improvements
Utilities must provide a cost-of-service study within 180 days of request showing how serving these customers affects cost allocation
Approved by the Governor June 4, 2026, filed with the Secretary of State June 5, 2026; provisions sunset/repeal December 31, 2033
policies.summary: Arizona HB 2756 (Chapter 111), approved June 4, 2026, gives the Corporation Commission authority to set contract and cost-recovery terms for large 'extra high load factor' electric customers like data centers, requires utilities to semiannually report new large-load interconnection activity and produce cost-of-service studies on request, and sunsets at the end of 2033.
policies.source_title: Arizona State Legislature — Session Laws, Chapter 111 (HB 2756)

policies.title: House Bill 4168 (Laws 2026, Ch. 140) — three-year pause on new Computer Data Center Program applications
key_terms: Bars the Arizona Commerce Authority from accepting new Computer Data Center Program applications, and bars new data centers from qualifying for the transaction privilege tax exemption, from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029
Established as session law (a temporary pause), not a permanent statutory repeal
Relief already awarded to previously certified facilities is unaffected
Estimated to preserve roughly $38 million/year in state revenue
policies.summary: Arizona's FY2027 budget bill HB 4168, signed by Gov. Hobbs June 13, 2026, pauses new applications to the state's Computer Data Center Program sales-tax exemption for three years (July 2026-June 2029) after public backlash over water and power use, while leaving already-certified facilities' tax relief untouched.
policies.source_title: Arizona State Legislature — HB4168 Bill Summary (57th Legislature, 2nd Regular Session)

resources.title: Arizona Capitol Times — Data centers dominated 2026 session

policies.title: Assembly Bill 1577 — data center reporting
key_terms: Requires data center owners/operators to submit location, size, power usage effectiveness and onsite-generator fuel consumption to the California Energy Commission
Requires disclosure to local agencies of expected annual energy consumption and expected sound levels
Commission must publish submitted data annually in anonymized, aggregated form on its website
Commission must assess data center electrical load trends starting with the 2029 integrated energy policy report and every two years after
Exempts publicly funded research, public safety, publicly funded national security, and publicly owned/utility facilities
policies.summary: Signed by Gov. Newsom Sept. 21, 2026 as part of a seven-bill data center package, AB 1577 creates a first-in-the-nation state registry requiring data centers to report location, size, power usage effectiveness, backup-generator fuel use, expected energy consumption and noise levels, with the California Energy Commission publishing aggregated results and tracking load trends starting in 2029.
policies.source_title: CalMatters Digital Democracy — AB 1577: Data centers: reporting

resources.title: Office of Gov. Newsom — Governor Newsom Signs Most Comprehensive Data Center Laws in the Nation

policies.title: Assembly Bill 2469 — data center water use disclosures
key_terms: Bars a city or county from approving any discretionary or ministerial permit for a new or peak-water-use-increasing data center expansion unless specified water disclosures are made
Requires a water supply assessment as part of the permit application
Starting Jan. 1, 2028, applicants must submit a water scarcity plan describing how the facility would cut water use under drought conditions
Developer must cover the full cost of any new water pipes, treatment or storage capacity the facility requires
policies.summary: AB 2469, signed Sept. 21, 2026, conditions local permit approval for new or water-use-expanding California data centers on disclosing a water supply assessment and (from 2028) a drought water-scarcity plan, and requires the developer to pay the full cost of any new water infrastructure the facility needs.
policies.source_title: Karmactive — California AB 2469 Could Delay Data Center Permits With New Water Rules

resources.title: Office of Gov. Newsom — Governor Newsom Signs Most Comprehensive Data Center Laws in the Nation

policies.title: Senate Bill 886 — California Technology Innovation and Ratepayer Protection Act
key_terms: Requires the CPUC to adopt new tariffs and update electric rules for data center interconnection and service by Jan. 1, 2028
Tariffs must prevent stranded costs for, or cost shifts to, non-participating ratepayers

Newly filed transmission/distribution tariffs must ensure data centers pay a reasonable share of wildfire mitigation/liability, electrification and other societal program costs normally collected from distribution-level ratepayers
policies.summary: SB 886, signed Sept. 21, 2026, directs the California Public Utilities Commission to adopt, by 2028, new tariffs and rules ensuring data centers pay their own grid-interconnection and service costs rather than shifting them onto other ratepayers, including a fair share of wildfire and other societal program costs.
policies.source_title: Data Center Dynamics — California lawmakers pass data center ratepayer protection bills, send to governor for approval

resources.title: Office of Gov. Newsom — Governor Newsom Signs Most Comprehensive Data Center Laws in the Nation

policies.title: Cheyenne, WY – rejected $50 million Microsoft community benefits agreement proposal
key_terms: Councilman Larry Wolfe proposed $10 million annually for five years (starting July 2027, ~$50M total) plus contractual terms on ~40 items (traffic, noise, wildlife, affordable housing) as a condition attached to a 3,500-acre annexation
Council rejected the amendment 8-3 on June 23, 2026 (support: Wolfe, Pete Laybourn, Mark Moody)
The 3,500-acre annexation for Microsoft's data center expansion advanced without any community benefits agreement attached (second of three required readings)
Mayor Patrick Collins, absent from the vote, had previously called the benefits proposal 'extortion'
policies.summary: A Cheyenne City Council proposal to condition a 3,500-acre Microsoft data center annexation on a roughly $50 million community benefits agreement ($10M/year for 5 years plus ~40 other contractual terms) was rejected 8-3 on June 23, 2026; the annexation itself advanced without any benefits agreement attached. Mayor Patrick Collins had called the proposal 'extortion.' Microsoft separately operates under Wyoming's Large Power Contract Service tariff and contributed over $11 million to the Laramie County tax base in 2025.
policies.source_title: Cowboy State Daily — Cheyenne OKs Huge Microsoft Annexation, Rejects $50M Community Benefits Deal

policies.title: House Bill 26-1030 — Data Center Workforce, Clean Energy, Grid Modernization, and Consumer and Environmental Protection Act
key_terms: Would have required certified data center operators to commit to a $250 million minimum investment within 5 years and break ground within 2 years of certification
Would have required compliance with craft-labor, apprenticeship-utilization and prevailing-wage standards
Would have required energy-efficiency certification, water-management strategies and backup-power standards
Would have granted a 100% state sales/use tax exemption for 20 years (renewable for 10 more years on continued compliance) administered by a 9-member oversight authority
Introduced Jan. 14, 2026 (sponsors Reps. Valdez/Duran, Sen. Mullica); postponed indefinitely by the House Energy & Environment Committee on an 11-2 vote (2026-05-07); bill status 'Lost'
policies.summary: Colorado's HB26-1030, introduced January 14, 2026, would have paired a 20-year data-center sales tax exemption with labor standards (prevailing wage, apprenticeship), energy-efficiency certification and water-management requirements, but was postponed indefinitely by committee vote on May 7, 2026 and did not advance.
policies.source_title: Colorado General Assembly — HB26-1030

policies.title: Columbia County, GA – Google (Kinetic Infrastructure Solutions) data center agreement
counterparties: Economic Development Authority of Columbia County
key_terms: At least $17 billion investment commitment — one of the largest private investments in county history — approved by the Economic Development Authority of Columbia County
Counterparty is Kinetic Infrastructure Solutions, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. (Google's parent company)

County goal: use data center revenue to eliminate its share of homestead property taxes (currently ~40% of the county budget, ~$25 million/year), contingent on a November 2026 referendum authorizing use under Georgia House Bill 439

Must comply with the county's Data Center zoning district: 500-foot residential buffers, 65-decibel noise limit, closed-loop cooling, ban on private wells, full-cutoff lighting, and decommissioning requirements
33 buildings across 3,500 acres in Harlem; Google separately occupies a planned 23-building, ~1,900-acre campus at White Oak Park in Appling
policies.summary: The Economic Development Authority of Columbia County, Georgia approved an at-least-$17-billion agreement with Kinetic Infrastructure Solutions (an Alphabet/Google subsidiary), with county leaders aiming to use the resulting revenue to eliminate the county's homestead property tax share, pending a November 2026 voter referendum under Georgia HB 439. The project must meet a dedicated data-center zoning code (buffers, noise limits, closed-loop cooling, no private wells).
policies.source_title: WRDW — Columbia County advances $17 billion data center deal

resources.title: WGAC — Columbia County Expects $40 Million Annually from Google Data Center Agreement

policies.title: CoreWeave: community benefits philosophy and Ratepayer Protection Pledge
key_terms: "Communities that make our operations possible should be able to share in the benefits without shouldering our costs."
Signed the U.S. Ratepayer Protection Pledge to "fully fund their own power supply and grid upgrades so electricity costs don't get passed along to everyday ratepayers"
States community commitment begins "before the first shovel and outlasts the construction crews"
policies.summary: CoreWeave has published a general community-benefits philosophy (conserving local resources, creating economic opportunity, staying accountable after construction) and is a Ratepayer Protection Pledge signatory. It does not publish a numbered, formal company-wide benefits framework the way Microsoft/QTS/Crusoe do; its most concrete commitments are site-specific (see the Lancaster, PA and Hammond, IN agreement records).
policies.source_title: CoreWeave Blog — Why Data Centers Should Strengthen Local Communities

policies.title: Crusoe: How Data Centers Benefit Local Communities
key_terms: "We cover our onsite power generation and any required infrastructure upgrades to avoid passing costs on to our neighbors."
"Our advanced closed-loop cooling systems do not consume or evaporate water to cool the equipment."
"We prioritize hiring local residents" via regional vocational programs and school-district workforce partnerships
Additional tax revenue "helps fund local schools, emergency services, career training, water infrastructure, and roads"
Dedicated community liaison assigned per site; "we are transparent and accountable"
policies.summary: Crusoe publishes a five-commitment, ongoing (evergreen, no single announcement date) company-wide framework — energy cost coverage, closed-loop water-free cooling, local hiring, tax-funded local investment, and a dedicated community liaison per site — covering all of its data center host communities. The page footer shows a 2026 copyright but no article publish date.
policies.source_title: Crusoe — How Data Centers Benefit Local Communities

policies.title: QTS $50 million Dane County community commitment
policies.jurisdiction: Dane County / Town of Vienna / DeForest, WI
key_terms: Initial $50 million community commitment for Dane County, with direct investment in DeForest and the Town of Vienna
Funds scholarships and workforce partnerships with Madison Area Technical College
Research partnership with University of Wisconsin-Madison and contribution to the Wisconsin Frontier Technology Platform
Support for local nonprofits and first responders
Announced alongside a proposed up-to-1,600-acre, multi-building campus (first phase: 5 buildings across 650 acres)
policies.summary: QTS announced a $50 million community commitment for Dane County, Wisconsin as it advanced zoning plans for a multibillion-dollar data center campus in the Town of Vienna/DeForest area, funding scholarships and workforce partnerships with Madison Area Technical College, a UW-Madison research partnership, and support for local nonprofits and first responders. Co-CEOs Tag Greason and David Robey issued the announcement. The commitment was made ahead of the DeForest Village Board zoning application, so it is proposed rather than a signed development agreement.

policies.title: Project Jupiter (Oracle) PILOT / Industrial Revenue Bond agreement
policies.identifier: Ordinance No. 367-2025 (IRB Adoption); Resolution No. 2025-96 (IRB Inducement)
key_terms: $360 million in PILOT (payments in lieu of taxes) direct payments over 30 years for schools, infrastructure, and local services
$50 million dedicated to Doña Ana County/Sunland Park water and wastewater system upgrades, including $10 million to Sunland Park via a grant program
More than $600 million in Gross Receipts Tax payments to the State and County over the project life

$6.9 million in supplemental community investments: $1.5M Boys and Girls Club of Las Cruces construction (paid Jan 6, 2026), $4M workforce development (due Dec 31, 2026), $250K desalination plant evaluation, $150K community college connectivity, $1M habitat restoration with annual payments through 2036
Issued via three Industrial Revenue Bond series (2025A, 2025B, 2025C); approved September 2025
policies.summary: Doña Ana County adopted an Industrial Revenue Bond ordinance and inducement resolution (approved September 2025; exact day not confirmed) for Oracle's Project Jupiter data center campus, structuring $360 million in PILOT payments over 30 years plus a $50 million water/wastewater fund and roughly $6.9 million in near-term supplemental community investments (Boys and Girls Club, workforce development, habitat restoration). The county reported nearly $80 million in tax revenue delivered by mid-2026.

policies.title: Effingham County, GA – OpenAI 'Project Camellia' community benefits commitment
key_terms: $80 million in community benefits over the project's life, directed toward schools, public safety, health care, utilities, workforce training, housing, veterans' services, and small business/working-family support
Up to $71 million in Codex AI-coding-tool credits for eligible Georgia college, community college, and technical school students
"Electricity rates will not go up for residents because of this project"; OpenAI pays the full cost of required infrastructure and electric-service costs
3.2 gigawatts of power from Georgia Power, delivered in phases 2028-2032
A future 'Georgia Community Compact' will translate community priorities into specific commitments with an annual independent public audit
$20 billion, four-building campus at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon
policies.summary: OpenAI announced $80 million in community benefits (schools, public safety, healthcare, workforce training, housing, veterans services, small business support) plus up to $71 million in Codex credits for Georgia students, tied to its $20 billion 'Project Camellia' data center campus near Rincon in Effingham County. OpenAI commits to paying the full cost of the 3.2 GW Georgia Power infrastructure so residential rates don't rise, and plans a forthcoming 'Georgia Community Compact' with an annual independent audit to formalize specific commitments — meaning the framework is announced but not yet a finalized, itemized agreement.

policies.title: House Bill 7031 — data center sales tax exemption threshold increase (15 MW to 100 MW)
key_terms: Raises the critical IT load required to qualify for Florida's data center sales tax exemption certificate from 15 MW to 100 MW
Extends the deadline to obtain an exemption certificate from June 30, 2027 to June 30, 2037
No grandfather clause: previously certified data centers under 100 MW lose the exemption
Passed Senate 32-2, House 93-7; provisions take effect July 1, 2025 except as otherwise provided
policies.summary: Florida's HB 7031, signed by Gov. DeSantis June 30, 2025, restricts the state's data center sales tax exemption to facilities with 100 MW or more of critical IT load (up from 15 MW) and extends the program's certification deadline to 2037, cutting off previously certified sub-100 MW data centers with no grandfathering.
policies.source_title: The Florida Senate — 2025 Bill Summary, HB 7031

policies.title: Frederick County, MD – rejected $110M Quantum Frederick community benefits agreement
key_terms: Quantum Maryland LLC (a Quantum Loophole/Catellus/TPG-affiliated entity) submitted a development rights and responsibilities agreement application September 1, 2026, offering >$110 million in community investments for the 2,100-acre, 17.4M-sq-ft, 2.4 GW Frederick Digital Campus

Proposed breakdown: $30M Carroll Manor Elementary School renovations; $40M community center/recreational space; $14.5M workforce development/career-technical education; $10.5M agricultural land preservation; $10M perimeter improvements/trails; $5M community solar project; $1M fire engine
Also offered to cut planned data center development ~20% and potable water use 80% once a reclaimed-water system comes online
In exchange, the county would have locked in the project's development/zoning rules for at least 8 years

County Executive Jessica Fitzwater rejected the agreement on September 15, 2026, objecting specifically to the 8-year zoning lock-in rather than the dollar amount, and extended the county's data-center-application pause to July 1, 2027
policies.summary: Frederick County, Maryland's proposed $110+ million community benefits agreement with Quantum Maryland LLC for the Frederick Digital Campus (which hosts Aligned Data Centers and Rowan Digital Infrastructure) was rejected by County Executive Jessica Fitzwater on September 15, 2026, just two weeks after the September 1 application — not over the dollar amount but because the deal would have locked in the county's zoning/development rules for 8 years. The county's pause on new data center applications was extended to July 1, 2027. No company_slugs are set: the developer and site tenants (Quantum Maryland/Catellus, Aligned, Rowan) are outside this dashboard's tracked company vocabulary.

Sponsored by Sen. Matt Brass
Passed the Senate March 6, 2026
Died in the House; did not reach Gov. Kemp's desk
policies.summary: Georgia's SB 410 would have repealed the state sales tax exemption for new (but not existing) data centers. It passed the Senate on March 6, 2026 but died in the House, leaving Georgia's data center tax exemption fully in force; Gov. Kemp has been a vocal supporter of keeping the incentive.

Skilled Trades and Readiness (STAR) Program provides career development opportunities
$10 million investment to help community nonprofits adopt generative AI
Improvements to power grids and water treatment facilities in host communities
policies.summary: Google publishes a recurring set of community-benefit programs tied to its data centers: teacher-training grants, the STAR workforce/skilled-trades program, a $10 million nonprofit AI-adoption fund, and local infrastructure contributions (power grid and water treatment upgrades). Site-specific commitments (e.g., Botetourt County, Lenoir NC) are layered on top of these company-wide programs.

Annual Community Impact Payments to the city, up to $4 million/year per secondary reporting (CoreWeave.com blog interview)
Funds "new city-wide infrastructure and quality of life initiatives" and the College Bound scholarship program ("help thousands of students in Hammond go to college")
180 MW, 450,000 sq ft facility at 301 Digital Crossroads Drive on a 25-acre parcel (former State Line Energy plant site)
Contingent on a finalized NIPSCO power agreement

The city's own announcement did not print the exact dollar figure; a $4 million/year figure for the payment (reported to fund up to two decades of full College Bound funding) comes from secondary reporting.

policies.title: Huntsville, AL – Meta North Huntsville expansion project agreement
key_terms: $750 million expansion (second campus, 250 acres) in the North Huntsville Industrial Park
Estimated $8.1 million return on investment to the City and school system, with an extra $8-10 million for local schools once complete
$2.8 million sanitary sewer extension, with Meta funding $2.5 million of it
50 new jobs required at an annual wage of at least $80,000 (exclusive of fringe benefits)
policies.summary: The City of Huntsville's project agreement for Meta's North Huntsville second data center campus (a $750 million, 250-acre expansion, buildings expected complete by end of 2022) is projected to return $8.1 million to the city and school system, growing to an extra $8-10 million annually for local schools, funded a $2.8 million sewer extension (Meta covering $2.5M of it), and required 50 new jobs paying at least $80,000/year. policies.title: Data Center Investment Tax Exemption Program (20 ILCS 605/605-1025)
key_terms: Requires at least $250 million in capital investment over a 60-month period
Requires at least 20 new full-time-equivalent jobs tied to data center operations or maintenance
New jobs' total compensation must equal or exceed 120% of the county's median full-time wage
Data center must achieve carbon neutrality or a green-building certification
20% tax credit on construction wages, but only in designated underserved areas
Exemption runs up to 20 years as renewable 5-year certificates contingent on continued compliance
policies.summary: Illinois's data center sales-tax exemption program, created by Public Act 101-31 effective June 28, 2019, conditions eligibility on a $250M+ investment, at least 20 jobs paid above 120% of county median wage, and a carbon-neutrality or green-building certification, administered via a certification/MOU process with DCEO. As of July 1, 2026 the department stopped accepting new applications under a governor's directive issued June 5, 2026 (tracked separately as il-tax-exemption-pause-2026).
policies.source_title: Illinois DCEO — Data Center Investment Tax Exemptions and Credits

policies.title: Governor Pritzker directive pausing new Data Center Investment Program agreements
key_terms: Directs DCEO to pause processing new Data Center Investment Program agreements starting July 1, 2026
Issued after the General Assembly failed to pass the POWER Act (HB 5513) reforms by the May 31, 2026 spring-session deadline
Agreements entered into before July 1, 2026 remain honored and unaffected
Governor cited energy affordability, grid reliability, water depletion and community impacts as the reasons a long-term framework is needed
policies.summary: Gov. JB Pritzker directed DCEO to stop processing new Data Center Investment Program tax-exemption agreements as of July 1, 2026, after the legislature failed to pass his requested data center reform package (the POWER Act) by the spring 2026 deadline. Existing agreements are unaffected; Pritzker said he would push the issue again in the November veto session.
policies.source_title: Office of Gov. JB Pritzker — Gov. Pritzker Pauses New Data Center Tax Incentives

policies.title: House Enrolled Act 1210 — data center local sales/use tax revenue sharing
key_terms: Authorizes a host county or municipality to require a payment of up to 1% of the state sales/use tax that would otherwise be exempted on a qualified data center's electricity purchases, to qualify for certain sales tax breaks
Applies to data centers whose permits/certificates are issued after the bill's effective date

A broader companion bill (HB 1333) that would have added an equipment PILOT and eased farmland siting rules stalled in the Senate; only the narrower electricity revenue-share mechanism became law via HB 1210
Gov. Mike Braun signed the bill March 12, 2026
policies.summary: Indiana's HB 1210, signed by Gov. Braun on March 12, 2026, lets host counties and cities require qualified data centers to contribute up to 1% of the sales/use tax they'd otherwise not pay on electricity purchases, as a condition of the local permit/incentive process. A broader bill (HB 1333) with a PILOT-on-equipment provision and farmland-zoning changes stalled in the Senate.
policies.source_title: Mirror Indy — At a pivotal moment for data centers, Indiana lawmakers take little action

policies.title: Senate Bill 98 — data center sales and use tax exemption
key_terms: Requires at least $250 million invested in eligible data center costs within 5 years of operations commencing
Requires creation of at least 20 new full-time jobs held by Kansas residents within 2 years of commencing operations
100% state and local sales/use tax exemption for up to 20 years under an incentive agreement
Requires a 10-year electricity purchase agreement with the serving utility
Requires a comprehensive water conservation plan
Requires Kansas Intelligence Fusion Center review/approval for cybersecurity and critical-infrastructure screening
policies.summary: Kansas SB 98, signed by Gov. Laura Kelly on April 24, 2025 and effective July 1, 2025, makes Kansas the 37th state with a data-center tax exemption: a 20-year 100% sales/use tax exemption conditioned on a $250M+ investment, 20 new Kansas-resident jobs, a 10-year utility power purchase agreement, a water conservation plan, and a state security/critical-infrastructure review.
policies.source_title: Kansas Department of Commerce — SB 98 Data Center Sales Tax Exemption

policies.title: House Bill 775 — statewide data center sales and use tax exemption expansion
key_terms: Expands the data center sales/use tax exemption from Louisville/Jefferson County to all 120 Kentucky counties
Exemption duration scales up to 50 years for a $450 million+ capital investment in counties with 100,000+ population
Lower tiers: $100 million minimum in counties with 50,000-100,000 population; $25 million minimum in counties under 50,000 population
All qualifying investment must occur within 5 years of preliminary approval
Became law without Gov. Beshear's signature
policies.summary: Kentucky's HB 775 (2025) expanded the state's data center sales/use tax exemption statewide to all 120 counties with population-tiered investment thresholds ($25M-$450M) and exemption terms up to 50 years for the largest projects; it became law without Gov. Beshear's signature. Beshear has since (August 2026) publicly called for rolling the incentives back.
policies.source_title: Stites & Harbison PLLC — Kentucky Vastly Expands Data Center Tax Incentives

resources.title: Louisville Public Media — Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear calls for ending state tax incentives for data centers

policies.title: Act 730 (HB 827) — data center sales and use tax rebate
key_terms: Requires certification by Louisiana Economic Development
Requires at least $200 million in investment and creation of at least 50 permanent jobs
State and local sales/use tax rebate on qualified equipment and construction costs for up to 20 years, with a possible 10-year renewal
policies.summary: Louisiana's Act 730, enacted in the 2024 Regular Session, creates a 20-year (renewable to 30) sales/use tax rebate for data centers that invest at least $200 million and create at least 50 permanent jobs, certified through Louisiana Economic Development. The program has since drawn scrutiny for locking in an estimated $81.6 billion in announced investment without the state publishing a revenue-loss estimate.
policies.source_title: LouisianAI — Louisiana Data Center Tax Incentives: Act 730, PILOTs, ITEP

resources.title: Invest in Louisiana — Louisiana's Data Center Incentives: Big Promises, Bigger Questions

policies.title: Lancaster, PA – CoreWeave community benefits agreement
key_terms: $20 million in payments to local causes over the agreement term, described as the first data-center-specific community benefits agreement in the US

policies.title: Act No. 41 (H.3309) — South Carolina Energy Security Act
key_terms: Defines 'data center' as any facility over 5,000 sq ft housing computer systems/servers/networking/storage equipment, including colocation and modular/containerized units
Requires special contracts for large-load customers (including data centers) to identify all new facilities/upgrades needed to serve them and address how the customer will cover infrastructure costs
Costs of increased fuel, generation and transmission substantially related to serving a commercial data center's demand must be recovered solely from that data center, not spread to other ratepayers
Provisions do not apply to a data center that was already an electric service provider's customer as of May 15, 2025 (grandfather clause)
Also authorizes annual rate-adjustment mechanisms and competitive procurement mandates for renewables/storage tied to 2023 integrated resource plans
policies.summary: South Carolina's Act No. 41 (H.3309), the Energy Security Act signed by Gov. McMaster May 12, 2025, requires new commercial data centers to bear the incremental fuel, generation and transmission costs their demand causes rather than spreading them to other ratepayers, via special utility contracts, with a grandfather clause for centers already served as of May 15, 2025.
policies.source_title: South Carolina Legislature Online — Bill 3309 (Act No. 41)

policies.title: Scioto County, OH – Google Franklin Furnace PILOT / tax abatement
key_terms: 75% property tax abatement for 15 years (company pays 25% of what property taxes would otherwise be)
Payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) of $500,000 annually, plus additional compensation based on total square footage
Approved by Scioto County commissioners around January 22, 2026
First phase: 500,000 sq ft data center on a 792-acre site, ~50 permanent jobs listed in the agreement
policies.summary: Scioto County, Ohio commissioners approved a 75%-for-15-years property tax abatement for Google's proposed Franklin Furnace data center, structured as a PILOT paying the county $500,000 annually plus additional square-footage-based compensation. As of the source date Google had not yet committed to proceeding with construction.
policies.source_title: WSAZ — Google's request for tax abatement on proposed data center approved

policies.title: Senate Bill 135 — Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens
key_terms: Applies to data centers with 10 MW or greater peak electrical demand
Requires data centers to ensure their water use does not overburden local water resources
Requires data center operators to pay for the electrical infrastructure costs attributable to their own demand
Prohibits the state from preempting local ordinances that limit, prohibit or otherwise regulate data centers, preserving municipal authority
A companion bill signed the same day (SD legislative bill number 26923) lets the Public Utilities Commission assess regulatory review costs to data center companies
policies.summary: South Dakota's SB 135, signed by Gov. Rhoden March 25, 2026 after a competing push for new data center tax incentives failed, requires 10 MW+ data centers to cover their own grid infrastructure costs, avoid overburdening local water supplies, and explicitly preserves local governments' authority to regulate or restrict data centers despite state law.
policies.source_title: KOTA Territory News — Data center restrictions signed into South Dakota law after push for incentives failed

policies.title: St. Joseph County, IN – AWS Community Enhancement Agreement (Project Rainier)
key_terms: Community Enhancement Agreement worth approximately $143 million, per County Economic Development Director Bill Schalliol, "on top of everything else that company is providing to the community"
County Council approved the economic development agreement 7-2 on August 13, 2024

Per secondary reporting, benefits include parks, schools/students, fire departments, road improvements, and utility upgrades; AWS separately expected to invest up to $7 million in surrounding road infrastructure
Campus (Project Rainier) estimated to bring ~400 full-time jobs plus ~600 additional construction-period jobs
Separately, AWS launched a $250,000 St. Joseph County Community Fund awarding grants to 31 local organizations (Feb 2025)
policies.summary: St. Joseph County, Indiana's council approved a Community Enhancement Agreement worth roughly $143 million with AWS as part of the incentive package for the $11 billion Project Rainier data center campus in New Carlisle, on top of other AWS investment. The agreement funds parks, schools, fire departments, roads, and utilities per county officials and secondary reporting, though the underlying agreement document's category-by-category breakdown was not found on a primary page in this pass. AWS separately runs an annual $250,000 St. Joseph County Community Fund grant program.

policies.title: Public Chapter 961 (HB1847/SB2128) — data center electrical infrastructure cost allocation
key_terms: Applies to a 'data center' (a building primarily containing electronic equipment to process, store or transmit digital information) projected to have 50 MW or more of peak electric demand in its first three years
Prohibits a municipality or electric utility from paying or absorbing the cost of electrical infrastructure built to serve a covered data center
Electric utilities may reimburse data center operators only under standard policies applied equally to comparable customers, and only if it doesn't raise rates for existing customers
Grants covered data centers the right to purchase power from in-state independent power producers, including direct behind-the-meter interconnection
policies.summary: Tennessee's Public Chapter 961 (HB1847/SB2128), signed May 18, 2026, bars municipalities and electric utilities from absorbing or passing along the cost of electrical infrastructure built to serve data centers of 50 MW or more, while opening a path for those data centers to contract directly with in-state independent power producers.

policies.title: Tulsa, OK – Meta Tax Incentive District / PILOT agreement
key_terms: 25-year Tax Incentive District agreement: Meta pays $62.5 million in lieu of taxes over the term
Annual 85% property tax exemption (Meta pays 15% of standard property taxes)
Remaining 15% collected is expected to exceed $36 million over the life of the agreement, benefiting Tulsa, Wagoner County, and Catoosa Public Schools
Meta covers all project-site costs including $25 million in public infrastructure improvements
More than 1,000 peak construction jobs and about 100 operational jobs ('Project Anthem', 2M+ sq ft, $1B+ investment)
policies.summary: Meta's 'Project Anthem' Tulsa data center operates under a 25-year Tax Incentive District/PILOT agreement approved by PartnerTulsa: an 85% property tax exemption in exchange for $62.5 million in PILOT payments over the term, with the remaining taxed 15% projected to exceed $36 million for the city, Wagoner County, and Catoosa Public Schools. Meta also funds $25 million in public infrastructure. Reporting places PartnerTulsa's approval and the project's public announcement in April 2026; no exact approval day was found.

policies.title: Senate Bill 6 — large-load interconnection and cost allocation
key_terms: Defines 'large loads' as 75 MW or more (PUCT may lower the threshold)
Large-load customers must disclose competing service requests elsewhere in Texas and report on-site backup generation capacity of 50%+ of proposed load
Requires an initial $100,000 transmission screening study fee and demonstrated site control

Large loads must contribute to the interconnecting utility's interconnection costs via PUCT-set financial commitment requirements (security deposits per MW, construction contributions, or advance payments)
New large loads connecting after Dec. 31, 2025 must install equipment letting ERCOT directly curtail load during firm load-shed events and emergencies
policies.summary: Texas SB 6, signed June 20, 2025, overhauls how large electric loads (75 MW+, including data centers) interconnect to the ERCOT grid: mandatory disclosure of competing requests and backup generation, a $100,000 screening fee, PUCT-set cost-contribution requirements so large loads help pay for the infrastructure they trigger, and mandatory curtailment/ride-through capability during grid emergencies.

policies.title: Executive Order 2026-03 — Higher Bar for Data Center Development
key_terms: Directs state agencies to ensure large data center projects do not increase net water consumption and to protect water quality, with specific focus on the Great Salt Lake
Directs agencies to protect utility ratepayers from bearing infrastructure costs needed to serve large data center projects
Directs agencies to minimize air-quality impacts on surrounding communities and mitigate wildlife impacts
Requires 'transparent, meaningful and thorough' public comment opportunities during state review
Effective immediately upon signing
policies.summary: Gov. Spencer Cox's Executive Order 2026-03 sets a statewide framework directing Utah agencies to weigh Great Salt Lake water impacts, ratepayer cost protection, air quality, wildlife and public engagement when evaluating large data center proposals. It followed public backlash over the Stratos data center project in Box Elder County, though it does not set numeric thresholds.
policies.source_title: St. George News — Governor signs executive order establishing higher standards for data center development in Utah

policies.title: HB 153 / SB 94 — data center siting sound-profile assessment
key_terms: Before approving a rezoning, special exception or special use permit for a new 'high energy use facility' (100 MW+), a locality must require the applicant to submit a site assessment examining the facility's sound profile on residential units and schools within 500 feet of the property boundary
Sets no decibel ceiling, no water cap and no minimum setback — the requirement is disclosure/assessment, not a hard standard
Water-impact assessment remains at local discretion rather than mandatory
policies.summary: Virginia's HB 153/SB 94, effective July 1, 2026, requires localities to obtain a sound-impact site assessment before approving zoning for a new 100 MW+ data center near homes or schools, but stops short of setting an enforceable noise limit, water cap or minimum setback.
policies.source_title: Roanoke Rambler — A Roanoke Delegate Helped Write Virginia's New Data Center Law

policies.title: House Bill 496 — data center water use reporting and disclosure
key_terms: Requires any water user that must register withdrawal/use data with the State Water Control Board, and that supplies water offsite to another person, to separately report total monthly potable and reclaimed water volumes provided to data centers holding a DEQ air permit
Reporting categories also separately break out domestic, commercial/industrial and other non-categorized water use
Delayed effective date of January 1, 2027
Chaptered April 13, 2026
policies.summary: Virginia's HB 496, chaptered April 13, 2026 with a delayed effective date of January 1, 2027, requires water utilities and other bulk water suppliers to separately report, by category, how much potable and reclaimed water they provide to data centers with a DEQ air permit, making data center water use publicly disclosed for the first time.

Sales tax exemption for data centers that qualify through equipment refurbishment expires effective July 1, 2026
Leaves the original construction/new-equipment data center tax exemption structure otherwise in place

policies.title: Warren County (Vicksburg), MS – Amazon Warren County Community Fund
key_terms: $150,000 committed to the Amazon Warren County Community Fund, with grants up to $10,000 for community projects (STEM education, sustainability, digital skills, culture, health/wellness)
At least 200 direct data-center jobs plus ~300 additional full-time-equivalent community positions

Workforce training: more than 6,500 learners/job seekers trained across Mississippi via AccelerateMS, Mississippi Development Authority, and community college partnerships (data center operations, fiber optic technician training, AWS pre-apprenticeship)
Uses previously authorized Mississippi Major Economic Impact Authority incentive legislation from Amazon's Madison County project; no new state funds required
$3 billion investment near the Port of Vicksburg

Partnership with Entergy to bring a new 600 MW solar project onto the grid
No-cost access to Google AI courses and Career Certificates for Arkansas residents via the Arkansas Department of Commerce, starting with University of Arkansas and Arkansas State University students
Part of a $4 billion Google investment in Arkansas through 2027, including the company's first Arkansas data center (five buildings, 1,178 acres, West Memphis)
policies.summary: Google announced a $25 million Energy Impact Fund with Entergy Arkansas for energy efficiency and affordability programs in Crittenden County, alongside a 600 MW solar partnership and free AI training/Career Certificates for Arkansas residents, as part of its $4 billion Arkansas investment anchored by a new West Memphis data center campus.

policies.title: Wilmington, OH – AWS Community Reinvestment Area / compensation agreement
key_terms: Upfront, unrestricted one-time payment of $1.5 million to the City of Wilmington
One-time $350,000 payment to the Port Authority of Clinton County
Over $1 million in new annual tax revenue to the city via PILOTs and municipal income taxes, plus $1 million in new annual revenue to schools
At least $25 million in new public infrastructure (sewers, water main, water tower, road improvements) at no expense to the city

policies.title: House Bill 2014 — Power Generation and Consumption Act
key_terms: Authorizes up to two 'microgrid' industrial business development districts (up to 2,250 acres each, on state or former coal land) where non-utility generators can sell power free of PSC rate rules, siting certificates and net-metering standards, provided 90% of the power stays in the district
Permits any power generation type (including nuclear, coal or gas-fired) within a certified microgrid/high-impact data center district

Prohibits counties and municipalities from adopting ordinances that limit creation, development or operation of a certified microgrid district or high-impact data center project (local zoning preemption)

Data center property and equipment is taxed at salvage value (about 5% of assessed value) for ad valorem property tax purposes, with the majority of that revenue directed to a state grid-stabilization/security fund rather than local governments
policies.summary: West Virginia's HB 2014, a governor's priority bill signed by Gov. Morrisey April 30, 2025, creates fast-tracked 'microgrid' industrial districts where data centers can build their own power generation largely outside PSC oversight, preempts local zoning limits on certified projects, and taxes data center property at a steeply discounted salvage value, with most resulting revenue flowing to the state rather than host localities.
